title: Two Bids That Hit the Budget
statement:
An advertiser wants to fill one ad slot pair with exactly its remaining budget. You get the list of incoming bids, in arrival order, and the budget. Find two different bids whose amounts add up to the budget exactly.

Write def solution(bids, budget) that returns [i, j] with i < j and bids[i] + bids[j] == budget. A bid cannot be paired with itself, but two different bids may have the same amount.

If several pairs work, return the one with the smallest j (the pair that is complete earliest in arrival order), and among those the smallest i. If no pair works, return [].

examples.why: The LeetCode 1 example 2. The trap: 3 + 3 = 6, but there is only one 3, and a bid cannot be used twice.
The LeetCode 1 example 3. Two different bids with the same amount are fine.
Pairs (0, 2), (1, 2) and (3, 4) all sum to 5. The smallest j is 2, and the smallest i with it is 0.

think.q: What exactly do you return when there are several answers or none?
think.a: Indices, not amounts, with i < j. The pair with the smallest j wins, ties go to the smallest i, and no pair gives []. The classic problem guarantees exactly one answer; here you must handle zero and many, so the tie rule matters.

think.q: Walk through [3, 2, 4], budget 6, one bid at a time. For each bid, what partner do you need?
think.a: Bid 3 (index 0) needs 3: nothing earlier. Bid 2 (index 1) needs 4: nothing earlier. Bid 4 (index 2) needs 2: seen at index 1. Answer [1, 2]. You only ever asked 'have I seen amount X before?', which is a lookup.

think.q: What is the first idea that works?
think.a: Two loops: for each j, try every i < j. With j outside, the first hit is already the smallest j and then the smallest i. Correct, but O(n^2): 100,000 bids is 5 billion pair checks.
Hash map of complements. Walk once; for each bid, look up budget - bid in a dict of amounts already seen. A dict lookup is O(1) on average, so the whole walk is O(n).

1. first_index = {} maps an amount to the earliest index with that amount.
  2. For each j, bid in enumerate(bids): if budget - bid is in the dict, return [first_index[budget - bid], j].
  3. Otherwise, if bid is not in the dict yet, store first_index[bid] = j.
  4. After the loop, return [].

Empty list and a single bid (both []). The same bid used twice (look up before you insert). Duplicate amounts (keep the first index, or you break the smallest-i rule). Zeros and a budget of 0. Negative bids and budgets. A later pair with a smaller i that must lose to an earlier-completing pair.

hints: For each bid you know exactly which amount would complete it: budget - bid. The question is only whether you have seen it earlier.
Keep a dict from amount to index of the bids you have passed. Look up the complement before adding the current bid, so a bid never pairs with itself.
Returning at the first hit gives the smallest j. For the smallest i, do not overwrite an amount that is already in the dict.
explain:
Example 4, [2, 2, 3, 1, 4], budget 5:

  • j = 0, bid 2, need 3: not seen. Store {2: 0}.
  • j = 1, bid 2, need 3: not seen. 2 is already stored, so keep index 0.
  • j = 2, bid 3, need 2: seen at index 0. Return [0, 2].

Returning at the first hit gives the smallest j, because every pair that ends earlier would have been found earlier. Keeping the first index of each amount gives the smallest i for that j. Had you overwritten {2: 1}, you would return [1, 2]. Sorting with two pointers also finds a pair, but sorting loses the original indices unless you sort (amount, index) pairs, and it costs O(n log n).
complexity: O(n) average time, O(n) extra space for the dict

talk: One pass with a dict from amount to earliest index: for each bid I check budget - bid in first_index, which is O(1) on average, so the whole thing is O(n) time and O(n) space.
Order matters: I look up the complement before I insert the current bid, so [3, 2, 4] with budget 6 never pairs index 0 with itself.
The tie rule falls out of the loop: returning at the first hit gives the smallest j, and if bid not in first_index keeps the earliest index for duplicates, so the smallest i.

Why not sort plus two pointers: it needs the original indices carried along as (amount, index) pairs, costs O(n log n), and makes the 'smallest j' rule harder. It wins only when the input is already sorted and memory is tight.
Python ints do not overflow, so budget - bid is safe even at plus or minus 2 x 10^9.
extensions: The bids arrive sorted (LC 167): solve it in O(1) extra space with two pointers from both ends.
Return every pair, or just the number of pairs, that hit the budget. How do duplicates change the count?
Three bids that hit the budget (LC 15): sort, fix one, and run two pointers on the rest, O(n^2).
No exact match is required: find the pair with the largest sum that does not exceed the budget.
Bids stream in forever and the question 'does any pair hit X?' comes at random times (LC 170): which side do you make O(1), add or find?
